claims.text: On 2026-01-07, the patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset after exertion, throbbing and diffuse, associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, engages in regular jogging, denies smoking or recreational drug use, and consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines; the patient's mother has type 2 diabetes and father has hypertension.

Initial vital signs recorded on 2026-01-07 included blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examination on 2026-01-07 revealed the patient was alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, intact motor and sensory function, normal reflexes, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 2026-01-07 showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 2026-01-07 showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 2026-01-07, the patient was diagnosed with Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and admitted to Neurology Ward B00 under Dr. Kevin Richard Martin.
On 2026-01-07, the treatment plan included starting oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and arranging MRI/MRA of the brain and cerebral vasculature for that evening.
On 2026-01-07, the patient reported persistent headache rated 7/10 with blood pressure of 150/92 mmHg; blood tests revealed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 2026-01-07, the plan was to continue nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours and start KCl 1 g orally twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
On 2026-01-07 at 20:00, the patient's GP, Dr. Ethel Joanne Duffy, was contacted to provide an update on admission and the preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 2026-01-08, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS; the patient reported headache severity reduced to 5/10, with blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, CRP 12 mg/L, and persistent mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L).
On 2026-01-08, the medication regimen was adjusted to nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, with a plan to repeat MRA in 48 hours and continue KCl 1 g twice daily.
On 2026-01-08, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 2026-01-09, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 3/10; blood tests from 2026-01-08 showed mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg.
On 2026-01-09, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 2026-01-09, the rehabilitation team assessed the patient, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 2026-01-10, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 2/10 with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg; mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted on previous tests.
On 2026-01-10, the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and perform a repeat MRA on 2026-01-11.
On 2026-01-10, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs, and demonstrated understanding of the information.
On 2026-01-11, the patient reported headache severity of 2/10 with blood pressure 125/78 mmHg; a repeat MRA was ordered to confirm resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-11 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS, and discharge planning was set for 2026-01-12.
On 2026-01-11, outpatient neurology follow-up was arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; the repeat MRA from 2026-01-11 confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-12, the discharge plan included nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks, and advice to avoid triggers.
On 2026-01-12 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss discharge, and a discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg once daily was communicated.
Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 documents amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
